A1.justification: Both complete 19-page PDFs describe the same STP convergence study. The equations, Table 1, Figures 1–3, and Appendix A are readable and can be reliably matched.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original simulations comparing STP, RGF, and GLD on a 500-dimensional quadratic, using 50 trajectories per algorithm and reporting outcomes in Figures 1–3.

after.justification: Section 6 retains these original simulations and their convergence results in Figures 1–3.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1's three-point update and the step-size prescriptions remain unchanged. The revised distribution examples concern theoretical specialization; the experiments already used unit-sphere directions in v3.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same 500-dimensional quadratic minimization problem. No datasets, tasks, or additional test scenarios are introduced in the main text or appendix.

E2.justification: Section 6 and Figures 1–3 retain the same comparators: RGF from Nesterov and Spokoiny (2017) and GLD from Golovin et al. (2020).

E3.justification: Both retain zero initialization, dimension 500, STP step sizes 4/t^0.51 and unit-sphere sampling, identical RGF/GLD settings, and the same gradient-norm evaluations against iterations and elapsed time.

E4.justification: The same final-gradient and rescaled best-gradient convergence illustrations are retained. Neither version introduces additional ablations, sensitivity analyses, robustness tests, or case studies.

E5.justification: Both specify 50 trajectories per algorithm and display trajectory curves. Seed information, confidence intervals, significance tests, and uncertainty-reporting practices do not change.

E6.justification: Figures 1–3 contain identical plot images, and the experimental findings are unchanged: STP and RGF perform competitively, STP is described as slightly better, and both outperform GLD.

T1.justification: Section 2 replaces the discrete-direction lower-bound example with a unit-sphere expectation example. Theorems 6–7 lose their K >= 1 specializations, and Remark 6 replaces Gaussian/coordinate examples with mu_D = 1/sqrt(2*pi*d), yielding revised strongly convex rate constants. The general theorem bounds, formal assumptions, and all Appendix A proofs remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction replace the advertised strongly convex factor 1 - mu/(dL) with 1 - mu/(2*pi*dL), with the corresponding almost-sure rate revision. The introduction also drops the best-known-complexities claim. The central contributions across the same three function classes remain.

C2.justification: The discussion of which distributions realize the dimension-dependent rates shifts from canonical-basis directions to unit-sphere directions; Remark 6 also removes the Gaussian specialization. Interpretations of the empirical comparisons remain unchanged.

D1.justification: Section 6 retains the same implementation descriptions and hyperparameters. Neither version adds hardware, execution-environment, or code/data access information.

R1.justification: The introduction removes its reference to Li and Orabona (2019, Theorem 1) when discussing last-iterate SGD convergence and withdraws the broad best-known-complexities positioning. The bibliography itself, including Li and Orabona, is unchanged.

P1.justification: Localized abstract edits replace 'arbitrarily close' descriptions with explicit epsilon and s ranges. Short introduction and distribution-example passages are edited, while section order, overall narrative, and appendix organization remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 receives small spacing and width adjustments and consistent minimizer notation. Text reflow shifts the figures upward on page 10; their panels, axes, legends, and captions remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: v4 removes the overstated coordinate-basis specialization and replaces Remark 6's Gaussian example with unit-sphere directions satisfying the bounded-direction assumption. Explicit rate ranges and revised strongly convex constants better align the headline statements with the general theorems. These are useful corrections, while the unchanged proofs and empirical evidence limit the overall improvement.
